questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-J \\ I & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-I \\ 2I & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6I.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6J \\ I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6(-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6I) \\ I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{37}+C\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2({e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2(\pi /2)}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{{e}^{-2(-\pi /2)}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{-\pi }}{5}-\frac{2{e}^{\pi }}{5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}({e}^{\pi }+{e}^{-\pi })\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3J \\ I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3({e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3I) \\ I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{3x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3\pi }}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-\frac{{e}^{3(0)}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3\pi }}{10}+\frac{1}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({e}^{3\pi }+1)\end{aligned}
$$
